narrative:
The model predicted an 82% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; you placed in the bottom decile, far below the average of accepted students who typically rank near the middle of their class. This low ranking strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 26 was the second most important factor. It sits well below the average of 37 among accepted applicants and also pulled the outcome toward not passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.8 was the third factor. While still below the accepted average of 3.23, it actually worked slightly in your favor by suggesting you might perform a little better than the other signals implied.

Taken together, these academic indicators created a clear picture for the model that the risk of failing the bar was too high to offer admission.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, while also working to improve your class ranking in future coursework. These improvements would most directly change how a similar model evaluates your application in the future.
